extracted.intended_audience: philosophers and scientists interested in the foundations of scientific method, causation, and conservation principles
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explicates criteria and conceptual standards for defining causation, distinguishing kinds of causal relations, and relating causal thinking to laws (including Conservation of Force) as presented in a philosophical treatise. Useful for applying or evaluating arguments about causes, laws of nature, and scientific explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as invariable and unconditional antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of anything (in the relevant sense) is 'the antecedent which it is invariably and unconditionally consequent'—not merely an antecedent that has always been followed by the consequent in past experience, but one believed to always be so 'as long as the present constitution of things endures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere historical succession from causation by testing whether the antecedent would still be followed by the consequent under all applicable conditions; sequences that are invariable only conditionally (e.g., day and night) are not true causes unless unconditionalness can be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity in causation means unconditionalness
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaningful element of 'necessity' in causation is unconditionalness: that which 'will be, whatever supposition we may make in regard to all other things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proposed cause, ask whether its succession of the effect would hold under all hypothetical changes of other circumstances; if not, treat the succession as conditional rather than causal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions versus causes: immediate vs remote antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerating conditions for a phenomenon, include present objects possessing given properties; some antecedents produce properties (capacities) in objects which later serve as conditions for other phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize 'states of preparation' or capacities (e.g., painted wall, prepared gunpowder) as effects of earlier causes and as present conditions for subsequent phenomena—thus distinguish the cause that produced a capacity from the immediate conditions that exist at the moment of the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating capacities/states as names for predicted future behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacities conferred on objects (their readiness to produce effects) are not necessarily substantive present facts but may be 'a name for our conviction that they will act in a particular manner when certain new circumstances arise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a purported 'state' is not material (as with paint collocation or gunpowder grain arrangement it sometimes is), treat it as a conceptual shorthand for expected future behavior rather than a separate ontological entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition variant: cause as assemblage of positive conditions (excluding negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: A convenient modification confines 'cause' to the assemblage of positive conditions without the negative; then the cause is the antecedent(s) 'subject to no other than negative conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical definitions, one may omit negative conditions and describe the cause as the minimal positive conjunction of antecedents that, without addition of positive extraneous circumstances, suffices for the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience distinguishes conditional from unconditional sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience itself teaches which uniformities are conditional and which are (so far as we can tell) unconditional; e.g., experimental knowledge of the sun shows day follows the sun's presence, not merely that night has preceded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled or critical observations ('experimentum crucis') and broader background knowledge to decide whether an observed succession is truly unconditional (causal) or derivative upon other antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture of laws: combined causes produce conditional uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: From a limited number of unconditional sequences (causes) there will result many conditional sequences when causes coexist; the co-existence (intermixture) of laws gives rise to additional invariable orders so long as the causes co-exist but not beyond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing observed uniformities, consider whether they arise from single unconditional causes or from the particular co-existence of multiple causes (which makes the uniformity conditional on that co‑existence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedence is typical but simultaneous causation is admissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Although cause is often antecedent to effect, there are cases where effect may commence simultaneously with its cause (or with no perceptible interval); what matters is that the occurrence of the assemblage of antecedent phenomena invariably commences the other phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insist on a measurable time-lag as logically necessary for causation; instead, use precedence when it is available to determine direction, but accept synchronous cases if the invariant relation is demonstrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuance vs reproduction of effects: causes may need to persist
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions necessary for first production of a phenomenon are occasionally also necessary for its continuance, though more commonly continuance requires only negative conditions; some effects are instantaneous and must be constantly reproduced by ongoing causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between phenomena that persist without continued presence of the originating cause (e.g., a made plowshare) and those that require the ongoing operation of the cause (e.g., illumination, pressure in a tube); frame causal explanations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple heterogeneous effects follow one phenomenon, speak in terms of properties/powers
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same phenomenon is followed by different sorts of effects (e.g., the sun producing light, heat, celestial motions), it is usual and useful to say each effect is produced by a different 'property' or 'power' of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the properties/powers language as an abbreviation to denote different sets of effects traceable to the same underlying agent, while remembering these are convenient names that don't add explanatory content by themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent (primeval) causes and limits on universal co-existences
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist permanent causes (primeval natural agents: sun, earth, elements, cycles) whose origin we cannot explain; because we cannot infer distribution of these causes across space, co-existences among their effects (except when traced to a shared cause) are not universal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat regularities that depend on the particular distribution of primeval causes as contingent and not candidates for universal laws unless independent evidence shows the distribution is lawlike.

rubrics_metrics.name: All non-primeval phenomena are consequent on prior collocations of permanent causes (determinism condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every phenomenon that begins to exist is an effect (immediate or remote) of primitive facts or combinations thereof; the state of the universe at any instant is the consequence of its previous state such that complete knowledge would (in principle) allow prediction of the subsequent history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a working determinist framework for scientific explanation: causal chains can be followed back to primitive conditions even if the practical computation of future states is infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existences among effects derive from identity or co-existence of their causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable co-existences among effects are results either of identity of cause or of the mere co-existence of their causes; there are no original or unconditional co-existences between effects of different causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing a law of co-existence among effects, verify whether it collapses to a common underlying cause or is merely contingent on the co-distribution of distinct causes; only the former yields independent, lawlike co-existences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of Force as empirical law of interchangeability and quantitative equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirically established facts show phenomena regarded as different sources of force (heat, electricity, chemical action, muscular action, momentum) are interchangeable in definite and fixed quantities, with equivalence between what disappears and what appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured equivalences (e.g., mechanical equivalent of heat) to treat different manifestations as convertible modes of the same conserved quantity; distinguish the empirically proven interchangeability from theoretical extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of Motion (higher-stage hypothesis) requires additional assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The stronger claim that Conservation of Force is Conservation of Motion (i.e., all force = motion) rests on hypothesis of molecular motions (and, historically, the ether) to account for heat, light, electricity etc.; part of the doctrine is hypothetical rather than purely empirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting conservation-as-motion, acknowledge the theoretical assumptions (molecular motions, ether) involved; treat the empirical conservation relations as secure while remaining cautious about ontological identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force properly defined as potentiality of motion rather than actual motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the motion later manifested need not be actually present (e.g., potential energy in raised stone or coal), force is better defined as 'Potentiality of Motion' rather than motion itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame physical explanations in terms of capacities or potentialities that can later be actualized, avoiding conflating present actual motion with stored potential that underlies future effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: In causal explanation include both the presence of a force and the necessary collocation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the assemblage of conditions constituting a cause we must distinguish two elements: (1) the presence of a force (the changing antecedent) and (2) the collocation or position of objects required so that the force may undergo the particular transmutation producing the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check both that the requisite active agency (force/change) is present and that the spatial/structural arrangement (collocation) is appropriate for that agency to produce the claimed effect; causal law is 'change produced by change' and needs both aspects.
